Mr. Speaker, I thank you for that remark, but I am speaking of the part of the motion-Of course the motion deals with many things. The government is being condemned for having failed in the task of fighting against inflation. Inflation is a product of a defective monetary system and of unemployment. That is what I was talking about. I believe that comes from the motion, and I quote:
(2) for failing to present to parliament new and effective measures such as granting at age 60-
This is because of the monetary system. Ministers have told us that it would cost billions of dollars to grant pensions at age 60. So I am discussing the possibilities of making our monetary system more flexible, and then we might consider lowering the pension age for those who would voluntarily accept that benefit. I quote paragraph 3 of the motion:
for not having paid a national dividend as a means to increase the buying power of Canadians in order for them to benefit by the surplus of production deriving from progress and technology;
We find in the motion what I talked about in my speech. I mentioned the guaranteed income. I mentioned the inquiry on minimum guaranteed income made by our friends in the other place, so dividend or guaranteed income is almost the same thing, only the word is changed. According to the dictionary, a dividend is a surplus, a return to shareholders on the production of some industries. I have always believed that Canadians were shareholders of the Canadian government. What is now unbelievable is that according to many of our politicians-
Then, I shall give someone else a chance. I thank the hon. members for their goodwill, their generosity in allowing me, a while ago, to complete my remarks. I think the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Tessier), when he came into the House, had obviously prepared me well. I wanted to explain to him what people think of the Social Credit party and its erroneous understanding of the system.
According to the concept of politicians of every stripe with whom I have occasion to discuss, not all but unfortunately the majority, according to them, from Champlain and the courageous men who planted the cross, the plough and civilization in the forests of Canada, to their successors who for three centuries have improved agriculture, built cities, developed road systems and all the wealth we see about us, according to them, those people instead of inheriting wealth, have inherited debts. It seems to me we could hear, at times, a voice coming from our forests, our plants, saying in parody: You shall pay your taxes and your debts by the sweat of your brow. That is what we want to change, that infamous system of slavery which has been maintained far too long.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT FOR ALLEGED NEGLECT OF ECONOMIC PROBLEMS
speechtext:
A day such as this, Mr. Speaker, which is officially known as an allotted day but more colloquially is called an opposition day, is very appropriately chosen. I would like to congratulate the Creditiste party
May 19, 1978

because they have done something that is very important. On an opposition day the idea is that the opposition parties attempt to identify the issues in Canada which are of some significance and which are probably being ignored by the government. I want to congratulate the Creditiste party, for having chosen the motion on a subject that is very important to all parties on the opposite side.
The basic clause in the motion we have before us reads:
That this House strongly condemns the government:
The important word there is "condemns", and there is no doubt that all of us on the opposite side are condemning the government. It is not only us on the opposition side, however, because only two weeks ago the government found that the people of Canada were condemning them as well, and consequently they backed off from an election.
In looking at the balance of the motion that is before us, it is obvious what the Creditiste party is aiming at, and that is condemning the government because of their failure to give serious consideration to the economic problems that are facing this country. When you look at the four parts to their motion, each and every one of them deals with the economy in one way or another. The economy is possibly the most important of the issues facing Canada today.
One might ask, what does the government think of the important issues facing Canada today? It was not very long ago when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was interviewed by the press, and as reported in the Ottawa Journal on April 18 in an article by Mr. John Best the Prime Minister was asked what he felt were his greatest accomplishments in the last ten years. The Prime Minister said firstly the "linguistic equality". That is what the Prime Minister thought was his main achievement in the ten years of his reign as Prime Minister.
The second thing was this:
Right next to language came a whole series of supposed accomplishments in the foreign affairs field.
If those are the two areas of priority for this government and the two areas the Prime Minister wants to brag about, having made the greatest accomplishments in linguistic equality and foreign affairs, it is no wonder this country is in a sad way and that the opposition is condemning the government. It is no wonder the people of Canada are finally coming to life and realizing what is going wrong with this country.
I would like to read the important parts of each clause in the motion and comment on each. The first one reads:
-for having failed at the task in the fight against inflation and unemployment-
To get evidence of that we simply have to go back to April 10 and the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) on the budget. I would like to quote from an article in the St. Catharines Standard by Charles Lynch. The heading of the article is "Budget is an admission of failure". It is a quotation from the minister himself.
"This is a time," he says, "for Canada to face our problems critically and realistically."
The Economy
He goes on:
-"we can see that we did not always use our good fortune wisely... We all come to expect too much of the economy. Governments increased their spending too quickly. The money supply was increased too fast."
It is obvious what the problems are when the minister himself indicates the difficulties this government has got the country into.
The second clause in the motion before us reads:
-for failing to present to parliament new and effective measures-
The government has presented some new measures, but the question is whether they are effective. They have presented bills such as the Canada Labour Code, the act to recapitalize CNR, the transfer of offenders, compensation for former prisoners of war, and language in the courts. There is not very much in there dealing with the economy at all.
One bill they presented about the economy had to do with the inauguration of employment tax credits. One of the most leading and active business people in my constituency who has a business which makes springs tells me that it is a complicated mechanism, that the extra tax he has to pay because of the tax credit is in no way meaningful to him and he is not going to bother applying for it.
I will skip the third part of the motion because it is dealing with Creditiste philosophy on economics and I personally do not understand it.
The fourth clause reads:
-for not having agreed to present new legislation that would have stimulated the consumption of Canadian products-
The government has failed to act in this area completely. I would like to read a quotation from the minister of finance of Manitoba. After he heard about this new measure of the government to give the sales tax credit, he said:
"The initiative to give a major sales tax reduction to all taxpayers in Manitoba is one to which all reasonable persons subscribe, provided it is done in a fiscally responsible manner," Craik said. "However, for a federal government whose spending continues to careen out of control to espouse such a major tax reduction-$1.3 billion-without concurrent and matching reductions in federal expenditures, represents fiscal irresponsibility of the highest order."
That is our complaint. We have a sales tax credit abatement but the government is still spending more and more money.
I would like to wind up by saying that if we are going to get at the real issues behind the economic difficulties facing our country, the one area the government must look at seriously, which it has failed to do thus far, is the philosophy of taxation. There are two basic philosophies. The first one is to tax people as we do now on the basis of ability to pay. In other words, you tax profits, you discourage production and so on. The other one is to tax on the basis of services received.
